We examine the operator defined by the fractional derivative $D_z^\alpha$ acting on $L^2(0,1)$, subject to the boundary constraints $y(0)=0$ and $y'(1)=0$, where $1<\alpha<2$. We establish that the eigenfunction system associated with the related fractional Schrödinger equation is complete provided the complex parameter $c$ adheres to the condition $|\arg c|<\frac{\pi}{2}\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2\alpha}\right)$.

Smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH) is a widely used numerical technique for solving continuum mechanics problems, yet its accuracy is heavily dependent on the selection of volume elements. This study examines the impact of varying volume element choices on gradient estimation accuracy. We introduce a new methodology for choosing these elements that significantly enhances gradient estimation precision. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach can be integrated into the standard SPH framework with minimal extra computational cost.

The demand for hyperspectral imaging is growing rapidly, yet acquiring such data remains costly and time-intensive. Consequently, numerous deep learning methods have been developed to estimate hyperspectral images (HSI) from standard RGB inputs. However, these existing models typically treat every pixel identically, overlooking the fact that different regions of an image possess distinct characteristics. To address this, we introduce a novel deep function-mixture network that incorporates pixel-aware mechanisms. Specifically, we develop a pixel-aware attention module to capture long-range dependencies and construct pixel-aware deep function mixtures to model local characteristics. By integrating both components, our approach effectively captures comprehensive spatial information. Furthermore, we introduce a novel loss function that leverages the inherent sparsity of spectral data to enhance mapping from RGB to HSI. Experiments on the WHU-RSUN dataset demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques, with ablation studies confirming the efficacy of our proposed modules.

The ability to predict the geographic location of street objects, such as traffic accidents or construction sites, is a vital component of the intelligent city infrastructure. This study introduces a novel approach to street object geolocation that leverages contextual geographic details to enhance the precision of the predictions. The proposed method utilizes a deep learning framework to forecast the coordinates of these objects by integrating diverse data sources, including satellite imagery, land use classifications, and points of interest. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. The authors also highlight the potential of this framework for developing a data-driven system to automate the geolocation of traffic incidents.

Dam reservoirs are vital for water storage, hydroelectric generation, and flood control, yet their classification remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data and the high diversity of dam types. To address these issues, this study introduces a novel metric learning approach designed to enhance classification accuracy by constructing a feature space where similar dam types are proximate while distinct ones are well-separated. By integrating this method with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), we developed a new framework for classifying dams. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms traditional classification techniques, achieving an 8.4% increase in accuracy. Furthermore, the analysis confirms that the quality of the learned metric space is a decisive factor in classification success.

This work establishes the relationship between continuous and partially linear retracts and QFS-spaces, deriving key QFS-space characteristics from these perspectives. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the category of QFS-spaces constitutes a coreflective subcategory within the category of continuous and partially linear retracts.

This paper outlines our submission for the POI type prediction multimodal track at the 2020 GeoAI Challenge. Our approach utilizes a multi-modal Transformer architecture to integrate POI descriptions with geospatial imagery. By employing a multi-head attention mechanism, the model learns to weigh the relevance of text and visual features, ultimately learning to distinguish POI types through their visual appearances. Our results achieved a macro F1 score of 47.21, which represents a 2.21-point improvement over the baseline.

This study investigates the link between the language used in earnings call transcripts and subsequent stock price movements. We posit that the textual content of these transcripts encapsulates the strategic vision of the issuing firm, making them a vital source for predicting future performance. To test this, we developed a model utilizing a set of semantic-derived features extracted from transcripts to predict future returns. Our findings indicate that this approach yields results that are highly competitive with models relying on standard financial metrics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the predictive power of these semantic features intensifies during market downturns.

This study examines the sensing performance of a wireless sensor network (WSN) where nodes exchange data via multi-hop routing to a central fusion center. The analysis focuses on a WSN composed of $N$ sensor nodes, each generating independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) binary data. These nodes transmit compressed signals to the FC using multi-hop routing, with the assumption that the communication range is sufficiently large to ensure network connectivity. The paper derives the asymptotic expression for the WSN's sensing error probability under the condition of large $N$. Furthermore, the study evaluates the impact of restricted communication ranges on sensing performance and demonstrates that, for sufficiently large ranges, the derived asymptotic expression remains a tight approximation.

We introduce novel quantum algorithms designed to estimate the trace of functions applied to the product of two Hermitian matrices. By leveraging quantum singular value transformation, our approach achieves query complexity that is logarithmic relative to the matrix sparsity. This method serves as a streamlined variation of quantum singular value transformation-based block-Householder reflection. Our solution effectively generalizes several existing techniques, including trace estimation, trace norm approximation, and sign function approximation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our framework can be adapted to estimate the determinant of a Hermitian matrix.

This study investigates the dynamics of compactons—solitons with compact support—arising from the nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring a nonlinear dielectric medium. By employing the method of moving frames, we analyze these objects' invariance under the equation's symmetries and derive their moving profiles up to a unique moving parameter. Our analysis demonstrates that compacton profiles are governed by the medium's nonlinearity and remain invariant regarding the moving parameter. Furthermore, we explore the asymptotic behavior of these compactons as the medium transitions toward linearity.

The Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT) serves as a comprehensive framework for describing new physics interactions involving Standard Model particles. This paper examines how these interactions influence the production of a $t\bar{t}b$ final state, a configuration highly valuable for Higgs boson studies. We analyze the contributions of dimension-6 operators to this process, considering both the Standard Model and QCD corrections. Our findings indicate that the relevant Wilson coefficients can be constrained with high precision in this specific channel. Furthermore, we evaluate the potential of future high-luminosity LHC runs to further tighten these constraints.

We introduce a novel rotation sensor based on the Sagnac effect, which utilizes a single-mode optical fiber wound into a planar spiral. This configuration is driven by a measurement protocol that leverages the fiber's sensitivity to rotation and temperature to achieve an enhanced rotation response. This approach enables the detection of rotations at a rate of 10 Hz with a precision of 0.001 degrees per second. Furthermore, the device demonstrates a linear response across a broad operating temperature range, from -20°C to 60°C.

The development of whole-cell models has recently accelerated due to major breakthroughs in computational power and the availability of extensive bioscience and medical data. These models are now being employed to investigate cellular processes, predict cell responses to stimuli, and design novel therapeutic strategies. However, the sheer volume of data and the intricate nature of the underlying biological mechanisms present significant hurdles. To address these challenges, we propose a new framework for constructing whole-cell models that integrates the latest advances in machine learning. This approach utilizes machine learning to infer the parameters of a modular, compartmental ordinary differential equation (ODE) system, which represents the cell's internal dynamics. We apply this framework to simulate the behavior of *E. coli* under various conditions, including the influence of the environmental surroundings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the framework's utility by simulating the effects of gene knockouts and analyzing the cell's response to glucose and lactose fluctuations.

This study introduces a novel image search system designed to retrieve images of a target object from a vast collection using a single view of that object as a query. While current state-of-the-art methods typically rely on multi-view queries to achieve high accuracy, they are impractical for real-world scenarios where acquiring multiple views is often infeasible. To address this, we propose a new framework that leverages the inherent relationships between views to enhance the effectiveness of single-image searches. Our approach utilizes a multi-view image encoder to extract features from an input image, followed by a view-specific auto-encoder that reconstructs the object from those features. We demonstrate that the auto-encoder's reconstruction output serves as a robust representation for the object, effectively capturing its identity. Furthermore, we develop a specific loss function to optimize the retrieval performance of this representation. Extensive experiments on the MS-COCO benchmark confirm that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study introduces a novel approach to seizure detection by integrating two established methods: multi-centroid and multi-pass learning strategies. The multi-centroid technique involves calculating the centroid of the feature space for both seizure and non-seizure episodes, followed by classifying new data points based on their proximity to these centroids. The multi-pass learning technique, conversely, involves iteratively training a learning algorithm on a dataset to detect seizures, then repeatedly using the identified seizures to augment the original set for subsequent training rounds. The proposed hybrid method was evaluated against standard algorithms using a dataset of 24 hours of continuous EEG recordings from a single patient, achieving a sensitivity of 98.4% and a false alarm rate of 0.002 false alarms per hour. These results surpass the performance of traditional algorithms.

The dark siren approach offers a promising method for determining the Hubble constant ($H_0$) using gravitational wave (GW) sources, such as binary neutron star (BNS) or black hole (BH) mergers, where the electromagnetic (EM) counterpart is not detected. This study evaluates the precision of the dark siren technique by analyzing the BNS event GW170817, assuming the EM counterpart was missed. We examine how the uncertainty in $H_0$ depends on the number of EM-undetectable BNS events, the inclusion of a single GW event with confirmed EM counterpart, and the use of a GW catalog combined with galaxy catalogs. Our analysis indicates that a minimum of 100 BNS dark siren events is required to achieve a $H_0$ measurement accuracy of 2\%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that incorporating galaxy catalogs alongside GW data can enhance the accuracy of $H_0$ measurements even with a small number of events.

QALD-9-plus is a new dataset designed to assess multilingual capabilities in Knowledge Graph Question Answering (KGQA) systems. It expands upon the QALD-9 dataset by incorporating English, French, and German translations of the original QalD-9 questions and the QalD-9 graph across these languages. This extension enables a comprehensive evaluation of multilingual readiness in KGQA models. We introduce a new method for translating natural language questions into multilingual SPARQL queries, which is then benchmarked against existing multilingual translation approaches. Our findings indicate that our strategy outperforms current methods in generating multilingual SPARQL queries.

We introduce a fresh approach to learning from data streams, termed "hindsight summarization." This method hypothesizes that minimizing the prediction errors observed after the fact (hindsight) with regard to past choices will reduce attended errors more effectively than traditional methods. By applying this principle to the context of summarizing data sequences, we developed the "Hindsight Summarizer" (HS) algorithm. This algorithm is designed to function within a setting where data arrives sequentially, and the learner must make immediate decisions without the benefit of hindsight. We demonstrate that the HS algorithm converges to the optimal solution in the limit, even when the underlying data distribution is unknown. Furthermore, we establish a link between the HS algorithm and the concept of regret matching, a known solution in game theory.

Deep learning models have demonstrated significant potential in medical image analysis, yet their generalizability is often compromised by implicit biases present in training data. This study introduces a novel approach to mitigate such biases by integrating the Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) framework with a conditional discriminator. The proposed method aims to enhance the generalizability of deep learning models by generating synthetic data that effectively neutralizes inherent biases. We specifically target and address biases arising from variations in patient demographics, such as age and gender, as well as from differences in clinical conditions. To achieve this, we employ a conditional generator that synthesizes images based on specific attributes, ensuring the resulting data distribution aligns with that of the original set. We have developed a new metric to assess the degree of bias in medical images and evaluate the success of the debiasing process. Experimental results indicate that our approach successfully reduces bias in medical images while maintaining the structural realism of the data.

Metric Learning (ML) is a critical component in numerous computer vision applications, including face recognition and person re-identification. While recent advancements in ML have been driven by the development of various loss functions, most of these approaches remain limited to either contrastive or metric-based methods, often neglecting the smoothness of the learned feature space. To address this limitation, we introduce Smooth Proxy-Achor Loss (SPAL), a novel ML loss function designed to enhance the smoothness of the embedding space. SPAL introduces a new proxy type that approximates the geometric relationships between feature pairs, enabling the generation of smooth embeddings. Furthermore, SPAL is a versatile loss function that can be integrated with existing ML techniques, such as contrastive or metric learning, to improve their effectiveness. Empirical evaluations on standard benchmarks demonstrate that SPAL consistently boosts the performance of state-of-the-art ML algorithms.

This study examines the statistical power of mark-weighted statistics for detecting cosmic voids by contrasting two distinct weighting schemes: density-based weighting, which is prevalent in current literature, and gradient-based weighting, which is proposed here. We demonstrate that mark-weighted statistics utilizing gradients are less influenced by the void's density profile shape, whereas density-based weighting depends heavily on it. Furthermore, we find that density-based weighting yields significantly tighter constraints on cosmological parameters compared to gradient-based methods.

We introduce a novel effective action for superfluids that incorporates external magnetic fields, derived from the effective action of charged bosons within a boson-fermion mixture. This effective action facilitates the calculation of mixed quantum-mechanical and hydrodynamical fluctuations, which are essential for computing the one-loop contribution to the free energy. Our derived expression aligns with the results obtained by the bosonization method.

MAPD (Methyl-amine-propyl-doped plastic) detectors are highly effective for detecting gamma rays, benefiting from their high light yield, high electron density, and high electron binding energy. These characteristics enable the detection of gamma rays with energies as low as 100 keV. This study details the development of a MAPD-based Compton camera prototype, which utilizes a 10 cm x 10 cm x 10 cm detector. The system employs a 3x3 array of 10 cm x 10 cm detectors, each equipped with a 16-channel SiPM, resulting in a total of 96 channels. The system's spatial resolution was evaluated using a 59.5 keV source from ⁵⁵Co, achieving a resolution of 1.5 cm FWHM. The angular resolution was assessed using a 511 keV source from annihilation photons, yielding a resolution of 1.8° FWHM.

We introduce a new approach to the Hilbert series of a graded ring utilizing section genera. This methodology proves instrumental in defining Gorenstein rings and identifying their codimension. We further investigate the generation of the canonical module within the framework of section genera and employ these concepts to characterize Cohen-Macaulay rings having specific Betti tables.

This study introduces a Bayesian framework for comparing broker algorithms within the context of transaction cost analysis. By modeling transaction costs as a realization of a stochastic process, we derive the posterior distribution of a broker's performance relative to a benchmark. This approach facilitates the calculation of the probability that an algorithm delivers superior results and establishes a credible interval for its expected effectiveness. To accommodate various broker types, the framework employs a generalized Gaussian process prior, with specific instances selected to suit different broker characteristics. The proposed method is demonstrated using both simulated data and actual transaction records from the S&P 500 index.

This study presents a broadly tunable add-drop filter based on a microring resonator featuring a piezo-electric actuator. By applying a lateral strain to the ring, the filter's refractive index is adjusted, enabling tuning across a wavelength range of 100 nm. This capability is achieved with a tuning sensitivity of 0.03 nm per unit of applied voltage.

We introduce a novel framework for constructing and analyzing disease models derived from online data, such as data from web searches. This approach enables the analysis of vaccination campaign impacts by comparing modeled infection rates against actual data. The method employs a state-space model to represent disease dynamics, using an Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm to estimate parameters. Results demonstrate that our approach yields accurate parameter estimates and effectively identifies significant variations in disease dynamics caused by interventions like vaccination.

This paper introduces PILC, a new framework designed for lossless image compression. It utilizes a hierarchical architecture that integrates a multi-scale encoder-decoder with a multi-branch transformer. The framework employs a multi-scale strategy to capture both local and global features, alongside a multi-branch design to integrate information from various sources. By leveraging a multi-branch structure, PILC effectively combines features from different dimensions. Experimental results indicate that PILC achieves superior compression performance, reducing file sizes by 1.18 times on average compared to PNG, with even greater improvements observed on specific image categories. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ChenYAN007/PILC.

This study reports a search for the rare decay $B^{+} \rightarrow D_s^{+}\gamma$ using $pp$ collision data from the LHCb experiment, collected between 2010 and 2012 with an integrated luminosity of 1 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on the $\Lambda_{\rm{reco}}$ region, defined by the decay of a $D_s^{+}$ meson into $\pi^{+}\pi^{-}\pi^{-}\pi^{+}$. Optimal transport (OT) has become a fundamental tool for measuring distances between probability distributions, yet standard OT metrics are highly sensitive to outliers. This paper introduces a novel framework called "outlier-robust optimal transport" (ORO), designed to mitigate such sensitivity. The core of the approach involves a penalty term that penalizes transport plans assigning mass to outlier regions, thereby encouraging the model to avoid them. The resulting optimization problem is non-convex and non-smooth, posing significant challenges for efficient resolution. To address this, we propose a new algorithm called "outlier-robust Sinkhorn" (ORSK), which is derived from the proximal point method. This algorithm guarantees convergence to a stationary point and is computationally efficient, allowing for the calculation of ORO distances with a speed comparable to the classical Sinkhorn algorithm. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that ORSK effectively estimates distances between distributions containing outliers. Additionally, we apply the ORO framework to a new task: "outlier-robust Wasserstein barycentric computation," which yields stable and efficient methods for determining ORO barycenters.

Human-Machine teams (HMT) are becoming increasingly common in both industry and research, yet current AI systems often fail to leverage human strengths, limiting their effectiveness. This study introduces a framework designed to help AI agents discover strategies that complement human capabilities, thereby maximizing joint performance. We apply this approach to a visual search task where humans and AI collaboratively locate multiple targets within an image. The AI is guided by human feedback to identify features that are complementary to human perception, and our results demonstrate that these agents achieve superior performance compared to those trained on standard supervised learning.

The spectrum of protons is a crucial indicator for the detection of potential proton decay. This study examines how the generation splitting (Spectrum Gens) spectrum influences proton decay, addressing the findings from the Super-Kamiokande experiment and projecting the capabilities of future detectors. We find that the spectrum Gens can be constrained by proton decay searches, with upcoming observations offering the potential to detect the spectrum Gens in a range of decay scenarios.

This study examines how individuals interpret pie charts, a visualization method that has seen little recent research despite its widespread use. We conducted a user study involving 100 participants from diverse backgrounds, including students, professionals, and non-experts, to assess their ability to analyze pie charts across varying levels of complexity. The results indicate that while experts and non-experts performed well with basic pie charts, they struggled with more intricate versions. Additionally, the study found that domain familiarity did not significantly influence performance. These findings offer valuable insights for designers aiming to create more effective pie charts.

This work introduces the concept of "clause set cycles," which are identified as the fundamental axiomatic structures underlying open induction, a formal system capable of defining concepts such as disjunctions and induction principles for linear orderings. We demonstrate that Kleinschmidt's axioms regarding well-ordering can be reduced to these cycles within open induction, thereby establishing the capability to prove Kleinsmidt's theorem via an automated theorem prover.

The Shortest Path Kernel (SPK) is a well-established kernel function for graph matching and retrieval, but it can be further adapted to enhance performance. This paper introduces a novel SPK variant that integrates the concept of node importance. We demonstrate that this approach can be realized through two distinct methods: a greedy algorithm and a dynamic programming technique. The dynamic programming method is presented as a new kernel for graph matching and is analyzed for its computational complexity. Additionally, experimental results on both synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that this enhanced SPK outperforms the original version and remains competitive with other state-of-the-art methods.

This study introduces a machine learning framework designed to simulate the transient dynamics of complex systems. The approach utilizes a neural network to learn a reduced-order model of the system's evolution, trained on data derived from a high-fidelity simulation. The training protocol employs a hybrid strategy combining batch learning with incremental learning steps. The efficacy of this method is demonstrated through its application to a two-dimensional Navier-Stokes flow problem. The findings indicate that the proposed framework can achieve high accuracy in simulating such dynamics, even when trained on datasets that are sparse in both spatial and temporal dimensions.

This study introduces an algorithmic framework for addressing power distribution issues, modeling the challenge through tools derived from fair division and division-by-the-cake problems. Specifically, we utilize the concept of connected components to define the electrical network and apply the MMS (Maximally Fair Share) fairness criterion to represent load balance requirements. Our primary contribution is a proposed method capable of solving distribution tasks across diverse scenarios, including those with limited resources, indivisible assets, and heterogeneous valuations. Furthermore, we establish theoretical upper bounds on the runtime complexity of this method. Finally, we validate our approach through numerical experiments, demonstrating its efficacy on test cases drawn from the IEEE 300-node bus system.

Event information collection is a critical task for event analysis, yet it frequently suffers from inaccuracies due to the omission of omitted event arguments. To address this, we introduce a novel approach leveraging event coreference resolution to enhance the precision of information gathering. The methodology utilizes a coreference resolver to identify coreferent groups within event descriptions and integrates these groups to forecast single-argument instances. Experimental results demonstrate that this process significantly enhances performance in event argument filling. Furthermore, we have developed a new evaluation metric to assess coreference prediction quality within the context of event information extraction. The study concludes by discussing the mutual benefits and synergistic effects between event coreference resolution and event argument forecasting.

The complementarity knapsack problem (CKP) extends the knapsack problem by incorporating special-structured complementarity constraints. This study introduces novel cutting planes for CKP, which yield a distinct family of facet-defining inequalities. We demonstrate the efficacy of these additions through computational experiments, showing that the new inequalities significantly enhance the performance of existing CKP solvers.

This study defines and examines generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan centralizers within $(m,n)$-torsion restrictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that imposing $(m,n)$-torsion restrictions allows for a derivation of generalized $(m,n)$-Jordan centralizers.

We investigate how Wigner constraints influence the Weinberg soft factor, which describes soft graviton emission from hard particles. Our findings demonstrate that incorporating Wigner constraints into the hard sector significantly alters the structure of the soft factor. We present a comprehensive calculation of the soft factor's contribution derived from hard particle spins, accounting for Wigner constraints. The resulting expression aligns with the Wigner constraint-free version up to terms proportional to the soft momentum, while introducing additional contributions proportional to the soft momentum squared.

This study examines the separation condition associated with the orthogonal projection of random linear combinations of $n$-dimensional unit vectors, alongside its extension to random projections defined by stochastic Gaussian matrices. The latter serves as a tool for establishing the transversal characteristics of certain nonlinear, projection-based operators. Additionally, within the context of random projections, we derive a refined lower bound for the second moment of the separation metric, thereby strengthening an earlier finding by Paouris and Pivovarov. Finally, we present applications of these theoretical results to optimization challenges, specifically addressing the global convergence of the proximal gradient method and the gradient projection technique.

Demonstration-efficiency constitutes a critical metric in Imitation Learning (IL), defined as the capacity to master a task using minimal demonstrations. This metric is vital for real-world applications, as gathering data is often expensive and time-consuming. While numerous IL algorithms have been developed to enhance this efficiency, their performance under distribution shifts remains largely unexplored. This study introduces a novel framework for evaluating the robustness of IL algorithms against shifts in the demonstration distribution. We validate this framework by analyzing the impact of distribution shifts on the efficiency of three prominent IL methods: Behavioral Cloning (BC), GAIL, and IQL. Our findings reveal that, contrary to expectations, IQL exhibits the highest vulnerability to such shifts, whereas BC and GAIL demonstrate superior resilience. Furthermore, we identify that the susceptibility to distribution shifts is closely linked to an algorithm's reliance on the demonstration set.

The intrinsic anomalous Hall effect (AHE) is a transport phenomenon driven by the Berry curvature of electronic states. While the second-order AHE has been observed in various materials, the third-order variant remains largely unexplored. This study predicts the emergence of a third-order AHE in non-centrosymmetric, non-polar crystals characterized by $C_{3v}$ symmetry, such as $\alpha$-Te, $\alpha$-Sb, and $\alpha$-Bi. Our analysis reveals that the $C_{3v}$ point group permits a non-zero third-rank AHE tensor component, $J_{3}^{3}$. Furthermore, we identify that the $C_{3v}$-symmetric materials $\alpha$-Te, $\alpha$-Sb, and $\alpha$-Bi exhibit a significantly large third-order AHE, with $\alpha$-Te demonstrating the strongest response. This finding establishes the theoretical groundwork for investigating the third-order anomalous Hall effect in materials governed by non-centrosymmetric crystal structures.

We present a novel approach to automatically generating execution summaries that highlight performance bottlenecks. Our method produces two primary artifacts: execution hierarchies and call graphs. These tools offer a comprehensive view of the execution environment, revealing the specific context of bottlenecks and their dependencies. We demonstrate that this technique is highly effective at uncovering performance issues, even within complex and dynamic environments.

We introduce a novel language modeling challenge designed to evaluate the capacity of systems to comprehend and detect anomalies within text. Our findings indicate that existing benchmarks fail to accurately assess true language modeling skills. To address this, we present the One Billion Word Benchmark, which utilizes a curated text collection that exhibits a higher perplexity than any previously evaluated dataset. Our analysis demonstrates that current state-of-the-art models struggle significantly with this data, achieving perplexity scores that are orders of magnitude worse than those obtained on established benchmarks.

This study examines the evolution of quasi-periodic sources in the 17 GHz range during the X2.2 flare event on August 7, 2014, using data from the Nobeyama Radioheliograph. The analysis reveals that brightness temperatures in these sources fluctuate between $10^{10}$ and $10^{11}$ K, with peak values reaching up to $10^{12}$ K. The source's spatial extent expands from approximately 10 arcseconds to 20 arcseconds, while the repetition interval of the quasi-periodic signals increases from 10 seconds to 30 seconds. These findings suggest that the quasi-periodic sources are likely associated with the 17 GHz source, which is linked to the flare's hard X-ray emitting region. The observed evolution of the quasi-periodic signals is consistent with the dynamics of the 17 GHz source, indicating a strong correlation between the two.

This study introduces a novel approach for detecting anomalies in images by applying statistical analysis to convolutional feature maps. The methodology involves training a convolutional neural network (CNN) on normal images, extracting feature maps from the network's final layer, and then utilizing a statistical test to identify deviations in these maps when analyzing anomalous images. The core premise is that feature maps effectively capture the essential characteristics of an image, allowing statistical procedures to detect subtle variations that signify anomalies. The approach employs a t-test to compare the distributions of feature values derived from normal versus anomalous data. Experimental results demonstrate that this technique achieves high accuracy in detecting anomalies across various image datasets.

Picard iterations fail to yield local well-posedness for dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev–Petviashvli I equations with small dispersion on the critical space $H^{s_c}$. This limitation arises because the Picard map fails to be contractive at the initial time step, a failure attributed to resonant interactions between the nonlinear term and the solution itself. To address this, we construct a refined version of the $X^{s,b}$-space tailored to the critical case, which successfully eliminates the problematic low-frequency resonant terms. Consequently, we establish the global well-posedness of the dispersion-generalized Kadomtsev–Petviashvli I equation with small dispersion in the critical space for dimensions $s_c < 1$.

This study examines the breakdown and subsequent recovery of Kramers' degeneracy in open quantum systems approaching thermal steady states. We demonstrate that within the thermal ensemble, the thermal doublet associated with Kramers' symmetry remains unbroken, even for Hamiltonians that do not explicitly preserve this symmetry. This resilience stems from the fact that the thermal density matrix is invariant under unitary transformations, a property that ensures the doublet's stability. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the violation or revival of this degeneracy in dynamical processes and the failure to reach thermal equilibrium. Specifically, we show that the degeneracy can be temporarily violated during the thermalization process, a phenomenon that can be observed through the emergence of a spectral gap in the Hamiltonian.

This study introduces a novel framework for wireless communication that integrates deep learning with artificial neural networks to enhance the efficiency of full-duplex systems. The proposed architecture utilizes a 3-D convolutional neural network (CNN) to forecast channel state information (CSI) by leveraging the spatial-temporal characteristics of signals. The resulting simulation results demonstrate that the 3-D CNN model achieves a 99.9% accuracy rate in predicting channel state information. The Gini, Atkinson, and Relative Theil indices are standard metrics for quantifying income inequality. While the Gini coefficient focuses on the average disparity between specific individuals and various incomes, the Atkinson and Relative Theil indices measure the disparity of the entire population relative to its mean income. This paper introduces a unified framework for these metrics, deriving a parametric family of inequality measures that encompasses all three. We demonstrate that, within this family, the dispersion of income is directly proportional to the dispersion of the population's cumulative distribution function. Furthermore, we establish that, under a specific transformation, the Gini function operates as the derivative of the Atkinson function, and vice versa. We also analyze the behavior of these measures under linear transformations of income and provide a proof of their equivalence.

The tempered spectral projection kernel $P_{\chi,\lambda}(z,w)$, which aggregates Laplace eigenfunctions with $\text{Re}(s)=1$, is analyzed for $SL(2,\mathbb{R})$ automorphic forms associated with a character $\chi$ of the center. This study establishes a decomposition of $P_{\chi,\lambda}$ into components arising from the continuous spectrum and discrete spectrum, alongside a holomorphic function $F_\chi(s)$ that encodes the singular behavior at $z=w$. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates that $F_\chi(s)$ is a meromorphic function with poles exclusively at $s=0$ and $s=1$.

The MARINLINGA algorithm is a novel method designed to reconstruct an initial graph from its corresponding line graph. Unlike prior approaches that depend on vertex or edge counts, MARINLINGA operates by first identifying vertices within the line graph that correspond to articulation points in the original structure. This discovery process is achieved through a heuristic algorithm that utilizes a specific property of these points. Subsequently, a graph reconstruction algorithm is applied to build the original network from the line graph's components. The paper demonstrates that MARINLINGA is capable of recovering the original graph from its line graph, even when the initial graph is not a simple tree.
The work explores the consequences of proving Lee-Lee's conjecture regarding the higher-dimensional Stasheff polytopes, which yields significant results for the genus formula of punctured discs.

Bloated dependencies are a prevalent issue in software development, where a package's API is expanded to accommodate new features, thereby increasing the API's size. This study investigates the persistence of bloated dependencies across 1,000 projects over 100 versions. Our analysis reveals that 70% of directly bloated dependencies remain bloated in later iterations, while indirect dependencies of bloated packages also frequently inherit this state. Furthermore, we demonstrate that bloated dependencies are prevalent in both open-source and commercial software. Our findings underscore the necessity for developers to assess dependency versions carefully to avoid inheriting or propagating bloated states.

This study examines the impact of quantum entangled bi-photons on the scattering of a mesoscopic polymer chain, revealing a distinct difference between this scenario and classical illumination. Specifically, one-way control (where the polymer induces a response in the scattered photons) remains independent of the initial entanglement between photon pairs, whereas reverse control (where incoming photons alter the polymer's state) exhibits a dependence. This latter effect stems from the entangled bi-photon's ability to generate vibrational excitations in the polymer, subsequently affecting the scattered photon's properties. Consequently, this phenomenon offers a novel pathway for quantum manipulation of soft matter, enabling the creation of quantum-controlled macroscopic systems.

Multistage distributionally robust optimization (DRO) is a powerful framework for managing uncertainty in complex decision processes. While recent research has focused on the first-stage decision in DRO problems, this study addresses the critical scenario identification problem for the complete problem. We introduce a novel methodology that utilizes a scenario tree to model the joint distribution of uncertain parameters across all stages. By leveraging this tree structure, we develop a computationally efficient algorithm to pinpoint critical scenarios in the first stage. The approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a supply chain network.

This study introduces a novel action anticipation framework that integrates a Spatio-Temporal Radial Basis Function (ST-RBF) kernel to model the dependencies between actions and context. The approach utilizes a multi-task learning strategy to enhance performance by concurrently predicting the imminent action, the timing of its occurrence, and the timing of the preceding action. The multi-task architecture is implemented through a shared convolutional backbone, with distinct branches for each prediction task. The model is further refined by optimizing a spatio-temporal Radial basis function kernel that captures the interplay between contextual cues and future actions. Experimental results demonstrate that this method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques, with significant gains observed in both overall accuracy and performance on long-tail action categories.

This work examines the emergence of thermalization in the context of holographic duality, specifically within the framework of black hole formation in anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime. We analyze how bulk black hole formation influences boundary observables, distinguishing between two scenarios: regular thermalization, where a single observable tracks the quasinormal mode spectrum of the final black hole, and deep thermalization, where multiple independent observables are required to capture the dynamics. We demonstrate that while these two regimes represent distinct physical processes, they can be reconciled by recognizing that thermalization is governed by the specific characteristics of the observables themselves.

This study introduces a new class of nuclear operators acting on specific function spaces generated by pseudo-differential operators. These operators are defined through infinite series comprising such functions. The work establishes sufficient conditions under which these nuclear operators exhibit specific characteristics within the given function space context.

This study examines the impact of the Line-of-Sight (LoS) condition on 5G deployments, specifically analyzing how it affects overall exposure to electromagnetic fields (EMF). The research evaluates the LoS condition for both downlink and uplink transmissions using a novel methodology that integrates a 3D ray-tracing model with a 2D cellular network simulation. The ray-tracing component calculates the LoS status for every individual ray originating from each base station and directed toward every user equipment node. Subsequently, the cellular network model incorporates these LoS conditions to simulate the overall exposure levels of the 5G network. The findings indicate that accounting for the LoS condition in 3GPP-compliant deployments results in a significant reduction in overall EMF exposure.

Code words, or Conceptual Distorted Embeddings (CODEs), are artificial anomalies inserted into training data to enhance a neural network's ability to detect and classify out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. This study introduces an efficient method for automatically generating CODEs and investigates their impact on the deep model's latent space. We demonstrate that CODEs effectively restructure the latent space to create a more distinct boundary between in-distribution and OOD regions. Furthermore, we show that these synthetic anomalies facilitate the identification of specific areas within the latent space that are critical for classification performance.

We present next-to-leading-order (NLO) calculations for the jet transverse momentum spectrum in the diphoton process, incorporating both photon-jet and double-photon-jet configurations. These results are benchmarked against experimental data from the LHC. The NLO predictions demonstrate a substantial enhancement in describing jet distributions compared to leading-order (LO) approaches, thereby refining the precision of background estimations. Additionally, we explore the potential for jet substructure refinement to further improve the accuracy of background modeling.

Recent advancements in self-supervised learning have significantly enhanced the ability of models to generalize on unseen data. This study investigates how leveraging unlabeled data can boost generalization in visual recognition tasks. We demonstrate that a straightforward yet effective strategy involves training a model on a mixture of labeled and unlabeled datasets, which improves generalization performance on unseen benchmarks. We further examine the impact of various data augmentation techniques on this generalization capability. The findings indicate that the model achieves superior results on the ImageNet-1k and ImageNet-1k+ datasets by training exclusively on the ImageNet-1k+ set with a data augmentation factor of 10x.

Outlier detection is a critical task in machine learning, yet it is frequently ill-posed because the distribution of normal data is unknown. While recent research has focused on enhancing the generalization of outlier detectors, these methods often fail to account for input feature dependencies. To address this, we introduce RECol, a novel approach that utilizes the conditional correlation between features to model their interrelations. RECol employs a two-stage process: first, it trains a conditional random forest to estimate the dependency structure, and second, it leverages these correlations to derive a more precise anomaly score. Experiments on various datasets demonstrate that RECol significantly outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, achieving improvements of up to 10% in AUC and 20% in F1-score.

This study examines a non-linear evolution equation defined on the half-plane, which models the vertical propagation of a viscous gravity current. We demonstrate that the regularity of the solution is directly determined by the regularity of the initial condition. Furthermore, our findings establish a phase transition in the asymptotic behavior of the solution, where the exponent in the exponential decay rate depends on the initial data.

The smallness of neutrino masses can be naturally explained by the Seesaw mechanism, which introduces heavy right-handed neutrinos. In this work, we examine the impact of these Seesaw neutrinos on the dimension-7 operator known as the Rayleigh operator. This operator, which violates lepton number by two units, is characterized by a dimensionless coefficient that is inversely proportional to the square of the mediator mass. Consequently, the Seesaw mechanism's heavy mediators naturally enhance the magnitude of this dimension-7 operator. We further investigate the constraints imposed by the latest cosmological data on the mass of the dimension-7 operator within this theoretical framework.

This study examines how short-term synaptic plasticity influences the generation of subthreshold oscillations and the emergence of bursting activity in a neuron model. We demonstrate that synaptically mediated short-term plasticity can both initiate and regulate these subthreshold oscillations, which are essential for the formation of complex burst patterns. Furthermore, we show that adjusting the strength of this plasticity allows one to control the frequency of oscillations and, consequently, the characteristics of the resulting bursts.

This study examines a spin-1/2 planar rotor interacting with a constant magnetic field within a specific gauge where the vector potential vanishes in the plane of rotation. By employing the Wu-Yang flux tube model, we demonstrate that the flux tube generates a non-trivial contribution to the system's Hamiltonian, resulting in an energy spectrum characterized by a two-fold degeneracy.

This study examines a one-dimensional Brownian particle constrained by a moving boundary, defined as $x(t) = x_0 + v t + \sqrt{D} W_t$ for $t > 0$. The analysis focuses on the collision count $N(t)$ and its statistical properties, specifically the probability distribution $P(N(t))$ and the mean collision frequency $\bar{N}(t)$. The results demonstrate that collisions accumulate linearly with time, scaling as $\bar{N}(t) \propto t$, in contrast to the case where the boundary is stationary. In the latter scenario, collisions follow a logarithmic time dependence, $\bar{N}(t) \propto \ln(t)$. Furthermore, the study establishes that the collision distribution $P(N(t))$ follows a Gaussian form for large $t$, with a variance proportional to the mean, $\text{Var}(N(t)) \propto \bar{N}(t)$.

We demonstrate that the set of formal knot groups for hyperbolic L-space knots is generated by five generators. Furthermore, we establish a second result showing that the set of formal knot groups for hyperbolic knot types is generated by five generators.

This work demonstrates that the compressible Euler equations for a gas, subject to an external potential, emerge as a hydrodynamic limit from the collisionless Boltzmann equation coupled with the Vlasov-Poisson system. The derivation applies to initial data characterized by bounded moments and compact support in velocity, provided the corresponding solutions to the kinetic system maintain their bounded moment properties over a finite interval.

This paper investigates the performance of multiple detectors when combined for real-time applications. We specifically analyze the YOLOv3 architecture, which is widely used in computer vision, alongside the ResNet50-based detector. Our findings indicate that merging these two models yields superior results compared to using either model independently.

Identifiers, such as variables and functions, are fundamental to code readability. Although numerous studies have examined naming conventions, few have explored how developers comprehend these names. This research investigates the impact of identifier naming patterns on a developer's mental model. We conducted a study involving 100 participants, who were shown code snippets with identifiers following specific patterns and asked to rate their perceived meanings. The findings indicate that certain naming patterns facilitate more accurate mental model construction than others. Additionally, we analyzed how mental models vary based on a developer's experience level and the domain context of the code.

This paper investigates the representation theory of the quantum algebra $B_n$ defined by generators $x_i, y_i$ for $1 \le i \le n$ and relations $[x_i, x_j] = [y_i, y_j] = 0$, $[y_i, x_j] = \frac{[q^{y_i} - q^{-1}][q^{y_{i-j}} - 1]}{[q]}$, where $q$ is a generic complex number. We establish that the unique nilpotent left $B_n$-module, denoted $\Delta_n$, is both irreducible and possesses dimension $q^n$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the quotient $B_n/B_{n-1}$ is isomorphic to the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. We also derive a basis for the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$. Finally, we prove that the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is isomorphic to the quantum group $U_q(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$.

This study examines the grain-growth dynamics in multiphase systems by analyzing the volume-fraction dependence of grain-growth rates for both the minor and dominant phases. Utilizing the Monte Carlo Potts model, we simulated the grain-growth process in two-phase systems, with each phase represented by distinct colors. The simulation domain was initialized with a square grid containing 1000 pixels, where the number of pixels assigned to each phase varied according to its respective volume fraction. The grain-growth rate was calculated by tracking the change in the minor phase's area over time, with the initial area defined as the number of pixels belonging to the minor phase at the start of the simulation. The analysis revealed that the isotropic grain-growth rate for the minor phase is governed by the volume fraction of the major phase. The study also explored the impact of varying grain-growth rates on the anisotropy of the system. The results indicate that the anisotropy of the system is influenced by the grain-growth rate of the major phase. Recent advancements in human mesh recovery have been driven by the availability of large-scale datasets featuring rich attributes, such as facial expressions, body poses, and skeletal structures. However, the impact of attribute selection on methodological performance remains underexplored. This study investigates how different attributes influence recovery outcomes, revealing that the effectiveness of a specific attribute set depends on the characteristics of the input data. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for human mesh recovery that dynamically selects the most suitable attributes based on the input data's properties. We further propose a new metric, the Attribute Importance Score (AIS), to quantify attribute significance. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed selection strategy significantly outperforms fixed-attribute approaches. Additionally, we conduct a comprehensive analysis of attribute importance across various datasets, offering insights into the efficacy of each attribute under different conditions.

We investigate the superconducting characteristics of a two-dimensional system with a square lattice structure, incorporating both electron-electron attraction and electron-phonon interactions. Employing the random phase approximation, we derive the self-consistent gap equation and the critical temperature for superconductivity. Our findings demonstrate that both the transition temperature and the critical magnetic field increase with stronger attractive forces; notably, the transition temperature exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on the magnitude of the coupling parameter.

We investigate the implications of dimension-6 operators within effective field theory regarding their matching to the Standard Model. We demonstrate that in the presence of these dimension-6 operators, the effective theory cannot be consistently matched to the Standard Model without incorporating the Standard Model's dimension-6 operators. We further establish a general formula for the coefficients of these dimension-6 operators in terms of the effective theory's Wilson coefficients. This work also addresses the model-independent constraints applicable to the Wilson coefficients of the effective theory's dimension-6 operators.

This guide serves as a gentle introduction to machine learning, designed for those with a mathematical background. It covers fundamental concepts, including gradient-based learning and the use of probability, by applying these techniques to analyze single and multiple linear regressions.

This study addresses optimal switching issues by examining terminal sliding mode control. Specifically, it demonstrates that terminal sliding mode functions as a specific instance of switching optimized to achieve minimal settling time. The analysis further reveals that this optimal switching strategy adheres to the maximum principle, with the switching function effectively representing a Lagrangian. Additionally, by applying the concept of topological duality, the research establishes that terminal sliding mode serves as the dual of this optimal switching problem.

This study introduces a novel ultrasonic resonance technique for characterizing the porosity of lithium-ion battery separators, highlighting its potential for non-destructive quality control within manufacturing processes. The research examines the impact of diverse separator dimensions and shapes on ultrasonic wave propagation, demonstrating that the resonance frequencies of these vibrations serve as indicators of the material's density. By applying these resonance frequencies, researchers can determine the separator's porosity. The authors also provide a comprehensive analysis of the experimental setup, including the characterization of the materials and the specific methods used to measure porosity via the resonance technique.

This study introduces a flatness-based control methodology for discrete-time systems featuring a state delay, extending the flatness concept to incorporate this specific constraint. The proposed framework includes a differential operator for the delay, enabling the derivation of a system model expressed in terms of shifted operators alongside the standard shift operator. The core methodology is illustrated through a case study of a discrete-time stirred-tank system, where the process is detailed. The analysis reveals that the flatness-based controller design procedure for discrete-time systems with delays differs significantly from the design process for continuous stirred-tank systems.

This paper presents a novel method for image captioning that leverages a small, high-quality curated dataset alongside large amounts of automatically generated data from the web. While current state-of-the-art algorithms typically rely exclusively on web-scale datasets, our approach utilizes the web-generated data to enhance the performance of models trained on curated inputs. We introduce a new architecture that integrates a recurrent neural network with a variational autoencoder, employing a teacher-student learning framework to transfer knowledge from the web data to the model. Our findings demonstrate that this combination yields superior image description quality compared to existing methods. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the proposed system's performance across various dataset sizes and image domains.

Let $n$ be a positive integer and $N$ be a number such that $N \ge n^2$. If $S$ represents a collection of binary strings of length $n$, the condition $|S| \ge n^2$ ensures the existence of a subset $S' \subseteq S$ with cardinality at least $\sqrt{n}$ where every pair of strings differs in their first $O(\log n)$ bits. This result establishes that for any $n$ and $N$, any family of binary strings of length $n$ with cardinality $N$ contains a subfamily of size at least $\frac{N}{n}$ having the property that all pairwise distances are at least $1 - O(1/\log n)$.

This paper demonstrates that any ordered Ehresmann semigroup functions as a generalized version of both one-sided and two-sided restriction semigroups, with these latter structures characterized specifically as those containing two mutually adjacent and compatible orders. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between the categories of one-sided and two-sided restriction semigroups and the class of ordered Ehresmann semigroups, achieved through their respective one and two-sided expansions.

This study investigates the relationship between the width of self-attention networks and their performance. We demonstrate that a network with 1 Trillion parameters and a width of 32,768 achieves a top-1 error rate of 21.0% on ImageNet-1k. We further prove that a width of 16,384 represents the optimal size for this model, as it yields the lowest validation loss.

The study investigates the optical and electronic characteristics of bulk BiFeO$_3$ alongside BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles, utilizing Density Functional Theory (DFT) and GW methods. The GW calculations reveal that the bandgap of BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles is approximately 1.5 eV smaller than that of bulk BiFeO$_3$, a finding that aligns with experimental data. Furthermore, GW calculations indicate that the bandgap of bulk BiFeO$_3$ closely matches the energy of the lowest absorption edge observed in experimental spectra. The study also examines the electronic structure of the surface states in BiFeO$_3$ nanoparticles, identifying a significant number of surface states within the bandgap. These findings suggest that the enhanced solar absorption in nanoparticles arises from the combined effects of the reduced bandgap and the presence of these surface states.

This study examines the $331$ model augmented with a $1-5-7$ generation structure. We demonstrate that the bottom quark and tau lepton masses originate from a novel symmetry-breaking mechanism, whereas the top, charm, and light leptons acquire mass through the standard Higgs mechanism. Furthermore, we analyze the resulting mixing patterns and discuss the implications for neutrino oscillations.

This study introduces a novel approach for reconstructing the 3D shapes of handheld objects from video sequences. By leveraging signed distances and an implicit neural network, the method effectively captures both fine details and global geometry. The proposed technique utilizes a single pass to reconstruct object shapes, thereby eliminating the need for iterative optimization. The entire process is end-to-end trainable, with the final object models represented as a set of signed implicit functions. The framework's performance is validated through experiments on synthetic datasets as well as real-world data.

We introduce Equal Contrast, a new method designed to analyze chromospheric variability by comparing high-resolution spectra taken at different times. This approach involves identifying a reference spectrum from the dataset, which is then used to normalize all other spectra. The resulting Equal Contrast maps reveal the temporal evolution of chromospheric features, offering a straightforward means to detect and quantify changes. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness using a 15-year dataset of 1,500 observations from the Swedish 1-m Solar Telescope, covering the solar cycle from 2007 to 2022. Our results show that the method successfully identifies the Sun's primary activity zones, including the equatorial belt, polar cap, and plage regions. Furthermore, we show that the method's performance is robust against the presence of active regions, which are often the main focus of chromospheric studies. By applying this technique to long-term time series, we can efficiently detect and quantify long-term chromospheric variability. We also provide an open-source implementation of the method, which is freely available for use.

This study reports a search for the decay mode $\Sigma^+\to p\pi^0\to p\gamma\gamma$ utilizing $4.7\,\text{fb}^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data collected by the LHCb experiment at center-of-mass energies of $7$ and $8\,\text{TeV}$. The analysis employs a likelihood fit to the invariant mass of the photon pair, with proton-pion and photon origins constrained by a vertex fit. The fitted signal yield is $10.0\,\pm 2.0\,\text{(stat)}\,\pm 0.8\,\text{(syst)}$, corresponding to a branching fraction of $\mathcal{B}(\Sigma^+\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\to p\pi\pi^0\

This study introduces a method for dynamically managing the workload assigned to workers in symbolic execution systems. By implementing test-depth partitioning, we divide the program's execution depth into layers, allowing workers to retrieve specific test cases from these layers. This mechanism enhances flexibility by enabling the system to adjust test allocation strategies based on the chosen partition depth. To further optimize efficiency, we developed an algorithm for depth-based test selection that prioritizes the most promising execution paths. Empirical results indicate that this approach significantly boosts the overall performance of symbolic execution tools.

This study examines the magnetization dynamics of a magnetic nanoparticle ensemble with anisotropy axes distributed along the equator of a sphere. The system is subjected to a static magnetic field oriented perpendicular to this distribution plane. The analysis focuses on the relaxation of magnetization and its dependence on the angle $\theta$ between the applied field and the anisotropy axes. The results demonstrate that the magnetization decay rate reaches a maximum when $\theta$ is $45^\circ$. This peak in decay corresponds to a minimum in the imaginary component of the susceptibility at $\theta = 45^\circ$, a finding that aligns with the predictions of the generalized Landau-Lifshitz equation.

Federated learning (FL) is a distributed machine learning approach that enables the training of a global model using data held locally on individual devices, eliminating the need for a central server. This paper introduces the Online Push-Sum (OPS) method, a novel distributed algorithm designed to aggregate local models into a global model within an FL framework. Unlike traditional methods, OPS operates without a central coordinator, making it ideal for decentralized settings. Theoretically, we demonstrate that the OPS method achieves an optimal convergence rate of $O(1/t)$ for both strongly convex and non-strongly convex problems. Additionally, we provide a numerical analysis confirming that OPS outperforms existing federated learning algorithms.

Dialog act prediction, a core component of dialogue systems, involves classifying the communicative function of a user utterance. Although recent advancements have significantly boosted performance, most current approaches rely on single-turn dialogue contexts, overlooking preceding short texts like emails or social media posts that often provide essential background context. To address this, we introduce a novel multi-task learning framework that jointly trains on dialog acts and task-bots' responses, enabling the model to leverage the context offered by short texts. Our proposed architecture utilizes a multi-head attention mechanism to integrate information from both the dialogue history and the preceding text. Experimental results on the ITC-GB 350k dataset demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods.

This device employs a 100 mm diameter, 100 mm long etalon with a 100 mm focal length, achieving a resolution of 100,000. The system is optimized for the 500 nm spectral band, featuring a 100 mm diameter field of view. The instrument's design ensures a stable etalon temperature, which is crucial for maintaining a consistent resolution. Codelets represent a proposed execution model designed to facilitate the heterogeneous integration of logic and memory within future chiplet-based systems. This work examines the codelet architecture, emphasizing the architectural and programming challenges inherent to codelet-based chiplets. It details a codelet-based chiplet model and introduces the codelet abstraction, which encapsulates the specific requirements for codelet implementation. Furthermore, the paper explores the advantages of codelet-driven heterogeneous integration and outlines the core principles of codelet programming.

Presmoothing is a nonparametric estimation technique that leverages smoothing to derive the nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator (NPMLE) within a specific subset of the NPMLE space. This paper introduces a presmoothing approach for survival analysis, specifically for estimating the cumulative hazard function in both independent and censored data scenarios. The method utilizes presmoothing to generate a consistent estimator that converges to the NPMLE as sample size increases. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that this estimator achieves higher accuracy than maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) under conditions of limited sample sizes. Furthermore, the study addresses censored data by employing the Nelson-Aalen estimator as the presmoothing foundation, accompanied by consistency proofs. The efficacy of these methods is validated through extensive simulations and a real-world application.

This study introduces the concept of nonlocal metric dimension, defined as the minimum cardinality of a nonlocal dominating set within a graph. We provide several characterizations for graphs where this dimension equals 1 or takes the value of $n(G)-2$. Furthermore, we determine the exact range of possible nonlocal metric dimensions for graphs possessing a nonlocal metric dimension of 1.

Power trace measurements are frequently employed in side-channel attacks to recover sensitive information from hardware. While existing research has successfully targeted cryptographic algorithms, this study investigates the viability of applying similar techniques to neural network architectures. We demonstrate that power measurements can effectively reveal the weights of a target model, even when the source code and the underlying hardware are not disclosed. Furthermore, we show that these trace measurements allow for the extraction of an approximating model that achieves comparable performance to a fully trained network.

This study introduces a new algorithm for shortening polarization kernels that relies on limiting partial distances. By utilizing these upper and lower bounds, the algorithm significantly reduces processing complexity compared to the conventional method of exhaustive enumeration.

This study introduces a new self-supervised learning framework designed to denoise seismic data. The approach leverages supervised training on a synthetic dataset to generate initial weights, which are subsequently refined using the original noisy data through a self-supervised learning algorithm. Experiments conducted on a real-world dataset demonstrate that the proposed method achieves comparable denoising performance to existing state-of-the-art techniques, while offering greater flexibility and lower computational costs.

This study investigates the impact of real photon emission on lepton-proton scattering, specifically focusing on the resulting charge asymmetry. We demonstrate that this effect is substantial and can be accurately modeled using a straightforward approach. The analysis includes contributions from both the proton's valence quarks and its parton sea. The derived predictions are compared against existing experimental data, and the discussion concludes with an examination of potential future measurement sensitivities.
